D     Exact reference families
Table 9 lists the families of Section 5.1. Below, Pr (X) denotes the probability that after r placements
the set of placed players is X, and the next-finisher rule is Equation (1): the next place goes to a
                                           P
remaining player j with probability sj / j ′ /∈X sj ′ . All dynamic programs start with unit probability
on the empty state, iterate this rule over r = 0, . . . , m − 1 on a compressed state, and accumulate
πr+1 times the probability that the queried player is placed at step r + 1.

Closed forms [4]. The first two places follow from the next-finisher rule, Qi,1 = si /S and
Qi,2 = j̸=i (sj /S) · si /(S − sj ), in O(n) per player. With flat prizes every player receives π; with
       P

equal stacks every equity is the mean prize. For linear prizes Vi = n + 1 − E[place of i], and under
                                                                         P
the exponential race P(Tj < Ti ) = sj /(si + sj ), so E[place of i] = 1 + j̸=i sj /(si + sj ), which yields
the formula of Table 9 (the term j = i contributes 12 ); mixed over the requested record this is
McCabe’s expected search cost [8, 23].

Dynamic programs. When the stacks take g distinct values with multiplicities n1 , . . . , ng , the
next-finisher rule depends only on how many players of each value have been placed, so the state
                                                      P
after r placements is a vector (x1 , . . . , xg ) with h xh = r. The next placement increments xh with
probability s(h) (nh − xh )/ h′ s(h′ ) (nh′ − xh′ ). A given player of value h is still unplaced in state x
                              P

with probability (nh − xh )/nh by exchangeability within the group, and is then placed next with
probability s(h) / h′ s(h′ ) (nh′ − xh′ ), so Qi,r+1 is the sum of Pr (x) times these two factors over the
                  P

states of layer r. Iterating over r < m costs O(m min(n1 , n2 )) for two values, the case used in the
suite. When all but e players have the same stack, the state is the set X of placed exceptional
players together with the count r − |X| of placed regular players, and the iteration costs O(m e 2e ).
For arbitrary small fields the state is the set of placed players; the layers r = 0, . . . , m − 1 contain
at most 2n subsets in total, so the iteration costs O(n 2n ) in total. The references are evaluated in
double-double arithmetic (Section 5.1); in plain double precision their own rounding error, of order
10−12 for the largest instances, would exceed the errors being measured.


Table 9: Families of exactly solvable instances used as references in Section 5. g is the number of
distinct stack values and e the number of exceptional stacks. DP denotes dynamic programming;
the references are evaluated in double-double arithmetic.

E     Validation suite
The suite of Section 5.1 uses the field sizes n ∈ {3, 10, 30, 100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000}.
Stacks. We use equal stacks; linear stacks, si = i; geometric progressions from 1 to 102 , 104 , 106
and 109 ; Zipf, si ∝ i−1.5 , and log-normal draws with σ = 2, both rescaled in the logarithm to ratio
109 when they exceed it; one stack 109 times smaller, or larger, than the n − 1 others; two stack sizes,
with one player, half the field, or all but one player at stack 1 and the rest at 3, 103 or 109 ; and ten
exceptional stacks among regular stacks of 1: spread over the ratio ρ, ρ−1/2+k/9 for k = 0, . . . , 9; all
below the regular stack, ρ−1/2+k/20 ; and all above, ρ1/20+k/20 .
Prizes. The structures are winner-take-all; two prizes with π2 /π1 = 0.5 and 10−6 ; flat over all n
places; linear, πr = n − r + 1; a realistic payout πr ∝ r−0.8 and a top-heavy payout πr = 0.7 r−1 ,
both for the top ⌈0.15n⌉ places; and satellites paying the top half of the field, the top 80%, or all but
the last player, equally. Each stack generator is paired with the prize structures for which Table 9
supplies an exact reference, and the small-field family (n ≤ 20) with all of them.
Runtime measurements. These use log-normal stacks with σ = 1, ratio capped at 106 , the full
prize vector or the top 0.15n places paid, at n = 100, 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000, and report the median
of three runs.
Random draws. The log-normal draws come from a 64-bit Mersenne twister seeded with 12345 + n
in the suite and 99 + n in the runtime measurements, passed through the normal distribution of the
C++ standard library; that transform is not fixed by the standard, so the draws are reproduced
exactly only with the GNU library used here, and in distribution with any other.
Extremal set. The sweeps of Section 5 run on 25 instances per field size, n = 100 to 4,000, chosen
from the error budget. For the discretization error: equal stacks with the full matrix and with prize
steps at 80% and 50% of the field, at a realistic payout and at the bubble; two-stack-size fields
whose largest equal group has n − 1 or n/2 members at ratio 103 ; and, because the relative error
of an equity can be large for a player whose equity is a single narrow transition of the group, a
tiny stack, or the ten exceptions below the group, among equal stacks under the 80% satellite. For
the truncation error: the geometric progression of ratio 109 , a single outlier of ratio 109 in either
direction, two-stack-size fields at ratio 109 and ten exceptions spread over the ratio, with the prizes
that expose the first, the second and the last place.
    At twice the step of Section 3.3, the largest absolute probability errors over the full suite and
the extremal set agree exactly for all six tested field sizes. The largest relative equity errors agree to
within 0.2%. In the full suite, the largest absolute probability error is attained by equal stacks with
flat prizes. The largest relative equity error is attained under the 80% satellite by equal stacks at
n = 100, and by equal stacks with a tiny stack or ten smaller exceptions at larger n.
